title: My, your, his, her
description: Say my, your, his, her, our and their with the right French form.

guide.summary: A French possessive agrees with the thing owned, never with the owner. Learn the six sets of forms and you can say whose anything is.

sections.title: What does the possessive agree with?
sections.text: The word for my, your, his, her, our or their changes with the noun that follows it, not with the person who owns it. The same car is sa voiture whether the owner is a man or a woman.
steps: Find the noun right after the gap: that is the thing owned.
Is it plural? Take the plural column and stop.
If it is singular, decide masculine or feminine and take that column.
Pick the owner’s row: je, tu, il/elle, nous, vous or ils/elles.

examples.en: His car is red. / Her car is red.

watch: The owner’s gender never shows: sa mère is his mother or her mother.
For nous, vous and ils/elles only number counts; gender is never a question.

sections.title: Mon or ma? Ton or ta?
sections.text: Before one thing, the possessive takes the gender of the noun. Learn every noun with its gender: the ending does not tell you (un parapluie, une chambre).
steps: Check the noun is singular: one thing only.
Recall its gender, un or une.
Take the owner’s row and the column for that gender.

examples.fr: Je lave ma voiture le samedi.
examples.en: I wash my car on Saturdays.

watch: A noun ending in -e is not automatically feminine: un parapluie, un livre.
The speaker’s own gender changes nothing: a woman still says mon sac.

sections.title: Several things owned
sections.text: As soon as the noun is plural, one form covers both genders.
steps: Look for the plural -s or -x on the noun.
If the noun is plural, take the plural form and forget gender.
When you rewrite a sentence, make the verb and the adjectives plural too.

examples.fr: Il appelle ses parents ce soir.
examples.en: He is calling his parents tonight.

watch: Ses (his, her) and ces (these) sound alike; only ses says whose.
The vowel trick belongs to singular nouns only: tes affaires, never ton affaires.

sections.title: His or her? French does not choose
sections.text: Son, sa and ses say nothing about the owner’s gender; the context does. Add à lui or à elle when you really must be clear: sa voiture à elle.

rows: son père = his father or her father
sa mère = his mother or her mother
ses sœurs = his sisters or her sisters
son amie = his friend or her friend

steps: Ignore the owner: man or woman makes no difference.
Look only at the noun that follows.
Take its line in the table.

examples.en: Julie is talking with her father.

watch: Her father is son père: père is masculine.
His mother is sa mère: mère is feminine.

sections.title: Before a vowel: mon amie, not ma amie
sections.text: Ma, ta and sa cannot stand in front of a vowel sound, so French uses mon, ton and son instead. The noun stays feminine, so adjectives still agree with it: mon idée est bonne.
steps: Check the noun is feminine and singular.
Say it aloud: does it open with a vowel sound or a silent h?
If it does, use the form that looks masculine; the noun stays feminine.
watch: A silent h counts as a vowel: son histoire, ton hôtel.
Plural nouns keep the plural form: tes amies, never ton amies.
Possessives never shorten with an apostrophe: no m’amie.

sections.title: Our and your (vous): only number counts
sections.text: Notre and votre serve masculine and feminine alike; only the number of the noun matters. Votre and vos are also the polite forms to one person you address as vous.
steps: Decide the owner: nous or vous.
Count the things owned: one, or more than one?
Take that cell; gender never comes into it.

examples.fr: Madame, vos billets, s’il vous plaît.

watch: Nôtre and vôtre, with a circumflex, are pronouns: le nôtre (ours). They never stand before a noun.
To a friend use ton, ta, tes; keep votre and vos for vous.

sections.title: Their: leur or leurs?
sections.text: Several owners take leur. The -s has nothing to do with how many owners there are: it appears only when the thing owned is plural.
steps: Check that several people own the thing: ils, elles, les enfants, mes voisins.
Count the things owned, not the owners.
Add the -s only when the noun is plural.

examples.fr: Les enfants jouent avec leurs chiens.
examples.en: The children are playing with their dogs.

watch: One car for the whole group is leur voiture, with no -s.
Leur in front of a verb is another word (je leur donne = I give them) and never takes an -s.

steps: Find the noun after the gap and check it is singular.
Decide its gender, un or une; the ending is not a reliable clue.
Take the owner’s row and the column for that gender.
Look at the noun: does it carry a plural -s or -x?
For a plural noun take the plural form and forget gender.
If you rewrite the sentence, make the verb and the adjective plural as well.
Ignore whether the owner is a man or a woman.
Look at the noun owned: masculine, feminine or plural?
Take the matching form of son, sa, ses.
Check the noun is feminine and singular.
Say it aloud: vowel sound or silent h at the start?
If yes, use mon, ton or son; the noun stays feminine for its adjectives.
Decide the owner: nous or vous.
Count the things owned; gender is irrelevant here.
One thing takes the singular form, several take the -s form.
Check that the owners are several people.
Look at the noun, not at the owners, to decide the -s.
Singular noun: no -s. Plural noun: -s.

exercises.instruction: Choose the word for my.
exercises.hint: Is chambre masculine or feminine, one or several?
exercises.feedback: Look at the noun chambre, not at the speaker.
exercises.explanation: Chambre is feminine singular and starts with a consonant, so my is ma.

mistakes.why: Mon stands before a masculine singular noun. Chambre is feminine, so a masculine form cannot sit in front of it.
Mes is the plural form, for several things owned. There is only one room here.

exercises.instruction: Choose the word for your (to a friend).
exercises.hint: Stylo is one thing. Is it masculine or feminine?
exercises.feedback: Match the possessive to stylo.
exercises.explanation: Stylo is masculine singular, so your (to a friend) is ton.

mistakes.why: Ta stands before a feminine singular noun. Stylo is masculine, so a feminine form does not fit.
Tes is the plural form, for several things. A pen is one object.

exercises.instruction: Write the French word for my.
exercises.hint: Think about the gender of voiture.
exercises.feedback: The possessive takes the gender of voiture, and there is only one car.
exercises.explanation: Voiture is feminine singular, so my car is ma voiture.

mistakes.why: Mon is the form for a masculine singular noun, and voiture is feminine (une voiture).
Mes is for several things owned, but the sentence washes one car.
Ta means your, not my. The subject is je, so the owner is the speaker.

exercises.instruction: Write the French word for your (to a friend).
exercises.feedback: Use the tu form that matches a masculine singular noun.
exercises.explanation: Sac is masculine singular, so your bag (to a friend) is ton sac.

mistakes.why: Ta is the feminine form, and sac is masculine (un sac).
Tes is the plural form, but the question asks about one bag.
Mon means my. The question is about what belongs to the friend you are speaking to.

exercises.instruction: Fix the error.
exercises.feedback: Parapluie ends in e, but that does not make it feminine.
exercises.explanation: Parapluie is masculine singular, so my umbrella is mon parapluie.

mistakes.why: That is the sentence unchanged. Parapluie ends in -e but it is masculine (un parapluie), so the feminine form in front of it is the error.
Going plural invents umbrellas the sentence does not have; only the gender of the possessive is wrong.
Son means his or her. The sentence says the umbrella is mine, and only the form has to change.

exercises.instruction: Build the sentence: My sister works in Paris. Leave one tile unused.
exercises.feedback: Only one word for my fits a feminine noun that starts with a consonant.
exercises.explanation: Sœur is feminine singular and starts with a consonant, so my sister is ma sœur.

mistakes.why: That tile is the masculine form, and sœur is feminine (une sœur). The tile you leave unused is the one whose gender does not match the noun.

exercises.instruction: Replace livre with lampe and change the possessive to match. Write the whole sentence.
exercises.source: Ton livre est sur la table.
answers: Ta lampe est sur la table.
exercises.feedback: The possessive must follow the new noun, not the old one.
exercises.explanation: Lampe is feminine singular, so ton becomes ta: ta lampe.

answers: Ton lampe est sur la table.
mistakes.why: The possessive still matches livre. Lampe is feminine, so the masculine form leaves the two words disagreeing.

answers: Ton livre est sur la table.
mistakes.why: That is the original sentence: livre was never replaced.

answers: Tes lampes sont sur la table.
mistakes.why: Nothing asked for a plural: one lamp replaces one book, so only the gender changes.

exercises.instruction: Choose the word for my.
exercises.feedback: The noun is plural.
exercises.explanation: Clés is plural, so my is mes. Mes works for masculine and feminine plural nouns.

mistakes.why: Ma stands before one feminine thing, and clés is plural.
Mon stands before one masculine thing. The noun here is plural, and in the plural both genders share one form.

exercises.instruction: Choose the word for your (to a friend).
exercises.hint: Look at the end of affaires.
exercises.feedback: The vowel rule for ton only applies to singular nouns.
exercises.explanation: Affaires is plural, so your is tes, even though the noun starts with a vowel.

mistakes.why: Ta is a singular form, and affaires is plural.
Ton replaces ta before a vowel, but that swap only happens with singular nouns. Affaires is plural.

exercises.instruction: Write the French word for his.
exercises.hint: Parents means more than one person.
exercises.feedback: For several things owned, his and her share one form.
exercises.explanation: Parents is plural, so his parents is ses parents.

mistakes.why: Son goes before one masculine thing, and parents means more than one person.
Sa goes before one feminine thing. The noun is plural, and gender stops mattering there.
Ces means these and only points at things; it does not say who they belong to.
Leurs belongs to several owners, but the subject il is one person.

exercises.instruction: Make chaussure plural and change the rest of the sentence to match.
exercises.hint: The possessive, the noun, the verb and the adjective all change.
exercises.feedback: Check all four words: possessive, noun, verb and adjective.
exercises.explanation: A plural noun takes mes, so ma chaussure becomes mes chaussures, with sont and sales.

mistakes.why: The possessive was left singular in front of a plural noun; it changes with the noun just like the verb and the adjective.
The verb and the adjective still describe one shoe, but the sentence now has several.
The adjective kept its singular ending; sale describes several shoes now.
That is the sentence unchanged: nothing was made plural.

exercises.instruction: Make ami plural and change the rest of the sentence to match.
exercises.hint: Plural nouns take a different word for your.
exercises.feedback: Change the possessive, the noun, the verb and the adjective.
exercises.explanation: Ami becomes amis, so ton becomes tes, est becomes sont and gentil becomes gentils.

mistakes.why: Everything went plural except the possessive, which follows the noun as well.
Only the first two words were made plural; the verb and the adjective still describe one friend.
Amies with an -e is a group of girls only, and nothing says these friends are female.
That is the original sentence, still singular.

exercises.instruction: Fix the error.
exercises.feedback: Sa only goes with one feminine thing.
exercises.explanation: Cousines is plural, so her cousins is ses cousines.

mistakes.why: That is the sentence unchanged: a singular possessive still stands before a plural noun.
Making the noun singular fixes the agreement the wrong way round; the sentence is about several cousins.
Ces means these; it points at the cousins instead of saying whose they are.

exercises.instruction: Translate into French.
exercises.source: My shoes are under the bed.
answers: Mes chaussures sont sous le lit.
exercises.feedback: Check the possessive: the noun is plural.
exercises.explanation: Chaussures is plural, so my shoes is mes chaussures.

answers: Ma chaussures sont sous le lit.
mistakes.why: The possessive stayed singular in front of a plural noun.

answers: Mes chaussure sont sous le lit.
mistakes.why: The noun lost its plural -s; both the possessive and the noun carry the plural.

answers: Mes chaussures est sous le lit.
mistakes.why: Est describes one thing, and several shoes need the plural of être.

answers: Mes chaussures sont sous la lit.
mistakes.why: Lit is masculine (un lit), so a feminine article cannot go with it.

exercises.instruction: Translate into French.
exercises.hint: The possessive matches père, not the woman.
exercises.feedback: In French, her does not have to sound feminine.
exercises.explanation: Père is masculine singular, so her father is son père.

mistakes.why: The possessive was matched to the woman who owns him. It agrees with père, which is masculine.
Grande is the feminine ending, and the adjective describes père, a masculine noun.
That gives her several fathers; the English sentence has one.

exercises.instruction: Translate into French.
exercises.hint: Look at the gender of mère, not of the man.
exercises.feedback: The possessive agrees with mère.
exercises.explanation: Mère is feminine singular, so his mother is sa mère.

mistakes.why: The possessive was matched to the man who owns her. It agrees with mère, which is feminine.
That makes several mothers, while the English sentence has one.
Towns take à; en is for feminine countries, like en France.

exercises.instruction: Translate into French.
exercises.feedback: For a plural noun, his and her are the same word.
exercises.explanation: Sœurs is plural, so his sisters is ses sœurs.

mistakes.why: Both of those forms stand before one thing, and the sentence has several sisters. In the plural, gender stops mattering.

answers: Ses sœurs sont à la école.
mistakes.why: École begins with a vowel, so the full article cannot stand in front of it.

exercises.instruction: Choose the word for his.
exercises.hint: Look at voiture, not at Marc.
exercises.feedback: Marc is a man, but the possessive does not care about him.
exercises.explanation: Voiture is feminine singular, so his car is sa voiture.

mistakes.why: Son is the form for a masculine singular noun. Voiture is feminine, and Marc being a man changes nothing.
Ses is the plural form, but Marc loves one car.

exercises.instruction: Choose the word for her.
exercises.hint: Look at père, not at Julie.
exercises.feedback: Julie is a woman, but the possessive does not care about her.
exercises.explanation: Père is masculine singular, so her father is son père.

mistakes.why: Sa is the feminine form. The possessive follows père, which is masculine, not Julie.
Ses is the plural form, and Julie is talking with one father.

exercises.instruction: Write the French word for her.
exercises.feedback: Match the possessive to portable, not to Léa.
exercises.explanation: Portable is masculine singular, so her phone is son portable.

mistakes.why: Sa is the feminine form, and portable is masculine (un portable). Léa being a woman does not matter.
Ses is the plural form, but she is looking for one phone.
Leur belongs to several owners, and Léa is one person.

exercises.instruction: Write the French word for his.
exercises.feedback: Match the possessive to chambre, not to Paul.
exercises.explanation: Chambre is feminine singular and starts with a consonant, so his room is sa chambre.

mistakes.why: Son goes before a masculine singular noun. Chambre is feminine, and Paul being a man changes nothing.
Ses is the plural form, but Paul tidies one room.
Ma means my, and the sentence is about Paul, not about the speaker.

exercises.instruction: Fix the error. Anne is calling her brother.
exercises.feedback: The possessive agrees with frère, not with Anne.
exercises.explanation: Frère is masculine singular, so her brother is son frère.

mistakes.why: That is the sentence unchanged: a feminine form still stands before frère, which is masculine.
That gives her several brothers; only the form of the possessive needs fixing.
Swapping the noun for a feminine one dodges the problem: the sentence is about her brother.

exercises.instruction: Choose the word for my.
exercises.hint: Amie is feminine, but look at its first letter.
exercises.feedback: Ma cannot stand right before a vowel.
exercises.explanation: Before a feminine singular noun starting with a vowel, ma becomes mon: mon amie. It still means a female friend.

mistakes.why: Ma is right before a feminine noun that starts with a consonant, but amie opens with a vowel and the two sounds cannot meet.
Mes is the plural form, and Claire is one friend.

exercises.instruction: Choose the word for your (to a friend).
exercises.hint: École is feminine, but look at its first letter.
exercises.feedback: Ta cannot stand right before a vowel.
exercises.explanation: École is feminine singular and starts with a vowel, so your school is ton école.

mistakes.why: Ta is the feminine form, but it cannot stand in front of a word that opens with a vowel, and école starts with é.
Tes is the plural form, and the question is about one school.

exercises.instruction: Choose the word for her.
exercises.hint: The h of histoire is silent.
exercises.feedback: A silent h counts as a vowel sound.
exercises.explanation: Histoire is feminine singular and starts with a silent h, so her story is son histoire.

mistakes.why: Histoire is feminine, so this looks right, but its h is silent and the word begins with a vowel sound.
Ses is the plural form, and she is telling one story.

exercises.instruction: Write the French word for my.
exercises.feedback: The feminine form cannot stand before a vowel.
exercises.explanation: Amie is feminine singular but starts with a vowel, so my friend is mon amie.

mistakes.why: Ma is the feminine form, but it never stands before a vowel sound, and amie begins with one.
Mes is the plural form, and there is one friend here.
Ta means your. Je te présente shows the speaker is introducing a friend of their own.

exercises.instruction: Write the French word for your (to a friend).
exercises.hint: Adresse is feminine and starts with a vowel.
exercises.feedback: Think of the vowel rule.
exercises.explanation: Adresse is feminine singular and starts with a vowel, so your address is ton adresse.

mistakes.why: Ta is the feminine form, but adresse opens with a vowel and the two sounds cannot meet.
Tes is the plural form, and you are asking for one address.
Mon means my, and the question asks for the address of the person you are speaking to.

exercises.instruction: Fix the error.
exercises.hint: Say ma amie aloud: two vowels collide.
exercises.feedback: Amie starts with a vowel.
exercises.explanation: Before a feminine singular noun starting with a vowel, use mon: mon amie.

mistakes.why: That is the sentence unchanged: two vowel sounds still collide between the possessive and amie.
That turns one friend into several; only the form in front of amie is wrong.
Possessives never shorten with an apostrophe in French; the whole word changes instead.

exercises.instruction: Build the sentence: His idea is very good. Leave one tile unused.
exercises.hint: Idée is feminine and starts with a vowel.
exercises.feedback: Look at the first letter of idée.
exercises.explanation: Idée is feminine singular and starts with a vowel, so his idea is son idée. Bonne still agrees with the feminine idée.

mistakes.why: Idée is feminine, so that tile looks right, but it cannot stand in front of a word starting with a vowel.

exercises.instruction: Translate into French. Julie is a woman.
exercises.hint: Julie is a woman, and amie starts with a vowel.
exercises.feedback: Check the word for my before amie.
exercises.explanation: A female friend is une amie, and before a vowel my is mon: mon amie Julie.

mistakes.why: The feminine form is blocked in front of a vowel; French keeps the feminine noun but changes the word before it.
Ami without an -e is a male friend, and Julie is a woman.
That is a plural, and the sentence introduces one person.

exercises.instruction: Choose the word for our.
exercises.feedback: Quartier is singular, and the word before a noun has no accent.
exercises.explanation: Quartier is singular, so our is notre. Nôtre, with a circumflex, is the pronoun in le nôtre (ours) and never goes before a noun.

mistakes.why: Nos stands before a plural noun, and quartier is one neighbourhood.
Nôtre with a circumflex is the pronoun in le nôtre (ours): it replaces a noun instead of standing in front of one.

exercises.instruction: Choose the word for your (formal).
exercises.hint: Billets is plural, and this is formal.
exercises.feedback: Use the vous form for a plural noun.
exercises.explanation: Billets is plural and the speaker says vous, so your is vos.

mistakes.why: Votre stands before a singular noun, and billets is plural.
Ta is the tu form, for friends and family. Madame is someone you address as vous.

exercises.instruction: Write the French word for our.
exercises.feedback: The singular form does not fit a plural noun.
exercises.explanation: Enfants is plural, so our children is nos enfants.

mistakes.why: Notre stands before a singular noun, and enfants is plural.
Nôtre with a circumflex is the pronoun le nôtre (ours) and never stands in front of a noun.
Vos means your: it belongs to the people spoken to, not to the speaker’s own group.

exercises.instruction: Write the French word for your (formal).
exercises.hint: One taxi, and the speaker is polite.
exercises.feedback: Use the vous form for a singular noun.
exercises.explanation: Taxi is singular and the speaker is formal, so your taxi is votre taxi.

mistakes.why: Vos stands before a plural noun, and there is one taxi.
Ton is the tu form, for friends and family, while Monsieur is addressed with vous.
Notre means our, but the taxi belongs to the man being spoken to.

exercises.instruction: Make voisin plural and change the rest of the sentence to match.
exercises.hint: Our has a different form before a plural noun.
exercises.feedback: Change the possessive, the noun, the verb and the adjective.
exercises.explanation: Plural voisins takes nos, with sont and sympathiques.

mistakes.why: Everything went plural except the possessive, which follows the noun too.
The noun lost its plural -s; it carries the plural just like the possessive.
The verb and the adjective still describe one neighbour.
That is the original sentence, still about one neighbour.

exercises.instruction: Translate into French.
exercises.feedback: Check the possessive for a singular noun and the ending of the adjective.
exercises.explanation: Maison is singular, so our house is notre maison, whatever its gender.

mistakes.why: Nos goes before a plural noun, and the English sentence has one house.
Petit is the masculine ending, and maison is feminine (une maison).
That describes several houses, while the English says one.

exercises.instruction: Build the sentence: Your suitcases are ready (you, plural). Leave one tile unused.
exercises.feedback: Choose the possessive for a plural noun.
exercises.explanation: Valises is plural, so your (you, plural) is vos.

mistakes.why: The singular tile was placed in front of a plural noun; the possessive follows valises.

exercises.instruction: Fix the error.
exercises.feedback: Notre only goes with one thing.
exercises.explanation: Amis is plural, so our friends is nos amis.

mistakes.why: That is the sentence unchanged: a singular possessive still stands before a plural noun.
Making the noun singular changes the meaning instead of fixing the possessive.
Nôtre with a circumflex is a pronoun (le nôtre) and never goes before a noun.

exercises.instruction: Choose the word for their.
exercises.feedback: Maison is singular.
exercises.explanation: One house shared by several owners is leur maison.

mistakes.why: Leurs carries the -s of a plural noun, but maison is singular. The -s follows the thing owned, not the number of owners.
Ses belongs to a single owner, and here several people share the house.

exercises.instruction: Choose the word for their.
exercises.feedback: Chiens is plural.
exercises.explanation: Chiens is plural, so their dogs is leurs chiens.

mistakes.why: Without the -s the possessive stands before one thing, and chiens is plural.
Sa belongs to one owner and one feminine thing; here several children own several dogs.

exercises.instruction: Write the French word for their.
exercises.feedback: The s depends on the number of dogs, not the number of neighbours.
exercises.explanation: Chien is singular, so their dog is leur chien, with no s.

mistakes.why: The -s was added for the several neighbours, but the possessive follows chien, which is one dog.
Son and ses belong to a single owner, and the sentence has several neighbours.

exercises.instruction: Write the French word for their.
exercises.feedback: The possessive must show the plural of parents.
exercises.explanation: Parents is plural, so their parents is leurs parents.

mistakes.why: Without the -s the possessive stands before one thing, and parents is plural.
Ses belongs to a single owner, but elles is several people.

exercises.instruction: Fix the error. Keep voiture singular.
exercises.source: Ils prennent leurs voiture pour partir.
answers: Ils prennent leur voiture pour partir.
exercises.feedback: The s on the possessive follows the thing owned.
exercises.explanation: Voiture is singular, so their car is leur voiture, without s.

answers: Ils prennent leurs voiture pour partir.
mistakes.why: That is the sentence unchanged: the possessive still carries an -s in front of a singular noun.

answers: Ils prennent leurs voitures pour partir.
mistakes.why: Making the noun plural keeps the -s, but the instruction says to leave one car.

answers: Ils prennent sa voiture pour partir.
mistakes.why: Sa belongs to one owner, and ils is several people.

exercises.instruction: Change il to ils, and make the verb and the possessive match.
exercises.hint: With several owners, his becomes their.
exercises.feedback: Change the subject, the verb and the possessive.
exercises.explanation: Several owners take leur; travail is singular, so it stays leur travail.

mistakes.why: The -s was added for the several owners, but the possessive follows travail, which is one job.
Son belongs to a single owner, and the new subject is several people.
The verb kept its singular ending after a plural subject.

exercises.instruction: Change elle to elles, and make the verb and the possessive match.
exercises.feedback: Change the subject, the verb and the possessive.
exercises.explanation: Several owners take leur, and cousins is plural, so their cousins is leurs cousins.

mistakes.why: Cousins is plural, so the possessive needs its plural form too.
Ses belongs to a single owner, and the subject is now several people.
The verb kept its singular ending after a plural subject.

exercises.instruction: Translate into French.
answers: Leurs enfants sont à la maison.
exercises.feedback: Check the ending of their.
exercises.explanation: Enfants is plural, so their children is leurs enfants.

mistakes.why: Without the -s the possessive stands before one thing, and children is plural.

answers: Ses enfants sont à la maison.
mistakes.why: Ses belongs to a single owner, while their points to several.
À la maison keeps its article; maison never stands bare here.

exercises.instruction: Build the sentence: They talk to their daughter. Leave one tile unused.
exercises.feedback: Choose the form of their for one thing owned.
exercises.explanation: Fille is singular, so their daughter is leur fille.

mistakes.why: The -s tile matches several owners, but the possessive follows fille, which is one daughter.
Parler needs à before the person spoken to: on parle à quelqu’un.
